name: Respiratory system
description: Larynx (thyroid cartilage), trachea, bronchial trees, the five lung lobes and the diaphragm.

source.anatomy_verified: Geometry and identity taken from BodyParts3D (FMA IDs preserved). Shapes simplified for the web only.
source.conversion_notes: Binary STL converted to GLB: vertices welded, meshes simplified with quadric decimation for web delivery, smooth normals, axes converted to Y-up/Z-anterior, recentred, one node per structure. Structures marked "merged" are the union of several BodyParts3D meshes (e.g. the parts of one muscle); structures with a "component" take one connected part of a BodyParts3D mesh, chosen by position.

groups.label: Respiratory system
groups.tip: Follow the air: voice box, windpipe, then bronchi that branch smaller and smaller, until they reach the tiny air sacs in the lung lobes.

groups.label: Airways
groups.tip: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more upright. So if you breathe in a peanut, it usually drops to the right.

groups.label: Lungs (lobes)
groups.tip: The right lung has three lobes and two fissures. The left has two lobes and one fissure, with a notch for your heart and a little tongue called the lingula.

groups.label: Diaphragm
groups.tip: C three, four, five keeps the diaphragm alive. Its phrenic nerve comes from these three neck nerves.

content.origin: From the Greek for shield-shaped. It guards the front of the larynx, your voice box.
content.location: It sits in the middle of the front of your neck, above the windpipe. It is the biggest cartilage of the voice box, and the smaller ones are not shown here.
content.description: Two flat plates meet at the front in a V-shaped ridge, the Adam's apple. The ridge is usually bigger in adult men.
content.function: It shields your vocal folds, which attach to the inside of its front corner. The voice box as a whole keeps the airway open, seals it when you swallow and makes your voice.
content.mnemonic: Thyroid means shield. Picture a shield on the front of your neck, guarding your voice.
content.clinical: In an airway emergency, doctors can open the soft membrane just below it to let air in. This is called a cricothyroidotomy.
content.hint: Find the shield-shaped cartilage forming the Adam's apple at the front of the neck, above the windpipe.

questions.text: The Adam's apple is formed by which structure?
questions.explanation: The two plates of the thyroid cartilage meet at the front to form the Adam's apple, also called the laryngeal prominence.

questions.text: What does the thyroid cartilage shield?
questions.explanation: Your vocal folds attach to the inside of the thyroid cartilage, which guards them like a shield.

content.origin: From the Greek for rough air tube. The rough part is the ridged rings you can feel in your neck.
content.location: It runs down the middle of your neck into your chest, below the voice box and in front of the food pipe. In the chest it splits into the right and left main bronchi.
content.description: A tube about 10 to 12 centimetres long, held open by 16 to 20 C-shaped rings of cartilage. Where it splits in two, there is a ridge called the carina.
content.function: It carries air between your voice box and your lungs. Sticky mucus and tiny hairs, called cilia, trap dust and sweep it up to your throat.
content.mnemonic: C-rings keep the airway open. The open side of each C faces the food pipe, so a swallowed mouthful can squeeze past.
content.clinical: A tracheostomy is an opening cut into the front of this tube to help someone breathe. A tension pneumothorax, a collapsed lung under pressure, can push it to one side.
content.hint: Find the ringed tube running down the middle from the voice box and splitting in two in the chest.

questions.text: What shape are the cartilage rings of the trachea?
questions.explanation: The rings are C-shaped. The gap at the back is closed by muscle, so the food pipe behind can widen when you swallow.

questions.text: Which structure lies directly behind the trachea?
options: Middle lobe of the right lung
questions.explanation: The oesophagus, your food pipe, lies right behind the trachea, against the open back of the C-shaped rings.

content.origin: From the Greek word for windpipe. It is called a tree because it branches like a tree turned upside down.
content.location: It sits in the right side of your chest, running from the end of the windpipe into the right lung. This one model shows the right main bronchus and all its branches.
content.description: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more upright than the left. It splits into three branches, one for each lobe, then into ever smaller tubes.
content.function: It carries every breath from your windpipe into your right lung. Rings of cartilage keep the big tubes open, like the ribs of a vacuum hose.
content.mnemonic: Right is wider, shorter and straighter, so a bite that goes down the wrong way goes right. Three branches for three right lobes.
content.clinical: If you breathe in a peanut, it usually drops into the right side, because this tube is wider and more upright. In asthma, its muscle squeezes the tubes narrow.
content.hint: Find the branching airway on the right, wider and more upright than its partner, with three main branches.

questions.text: If you breathe in a peanut, where is it most likely to get stuck?
questions.explanation: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more upright, so things that go down the wrong way tend to go right.

questions.text: How many lobar branches does the right main bronchus give off?
questions.explanation: The right main bronchus splits into three lobar bronchi, one for each lobe of the right lung.

content.origin: From the Greek word for windpipe. Like its partner, it branches like an upside-down tree.
content.location: It sits in the left side of your chest, from the end of the windpipe into the left lung. It passes under the arch of the aorta and in front of the food pipe.
content.description: The left main bronchus is narrower, longer and flatter than the right. It splits into two branches, upper and lower, then into ever smaller tubes.
content.function: It carries air from your windpipe to every part of your left lung. Cartilage keeps the bigger tubes open, and muscle in the walls adjusts how wide they are.
content.mnemonic: Left is longer and leans flatter to make room for the heart. Two branches for two left lobes.
content.clinical: Breathed-in objects end up here less often than on the right. Bronchitis is swelling of the lining of these tubes, causing cough and mucus.
content.hint: Find the branching airway on the left, longer and flatter than its partner, with two main branches.

content.origin: From the Greek for a rounded flap, as in an ear lobe.
content.location: It is the top part of the right lung. Its rounded tip rises just above your collarbone, into the base of the neck.
content.description: A wedge-shaped lobe. The right lung has three lobes, upper, middle and lower, and the horizontal fissure separates this one from the middle lobe.
content.function: Like every lobe, it is spongy tissue packed with tiny air sacs. There, oxygen passes into your blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
content.mnemonic: Right lung: three lobes and two fissures, one horizontal and one slanting. Think of three rooms and two walls.
content.clinical: A Pancoast tumour is a lung cancer at the very top that can press on nerves to the arm. Tuberculosis that flares up again usually strikes the upper lobes.
content.hint: Find the top lobe of the right lung, whose tip reaches above the collarbone.

questions.text: How many lobes does the right lung have?
questions.explanation: The right lung has three lobes: upper, middle and lower.

questions.text: Which fissure separates the upper and middle lobes of the right lung?
questions.explanation: The horizontal fissure runs across the right lung only. It divides the upper lobe from the middle lobe.

content.origin: From the Greek for a rounded flap, and the Latin for middle.
content.location: It sits at the front of the right lung, below the horizontal fissure. It rests against the right side of the heart.
content.description: The smallest lobe of the right lung, shaped like a wedge. Only the right lung has a middle lobe.
content.function: It swaps oxygen and carbon dioxide like the other lobes. To hear it with a stethoscope, listen on the front of the right chest, not the back.
content.mnemonic: Middle lobe, right side only. The left lung has a little tongue, the lingula, in its place.
content.clinical: Pneumonia here can blur the right edge of the heart on a chest X-ray. Doctors call this the silhouette sign.
content.hint: Find the small front lobe found only in the right lung, lying against the heart.

questions.text: Which part of the left lung matches the right middle lobe?
options: The lingula of the upper lobe
The tip of the lower lobe
questions.explanation: The left lung has no middle lobe. Instead, a tongue-shaped flap of its upper lobe, the lingula, sits in the same place.

questions.text: Pneumonia in the right middle lobe may blur which outline on a chest X-ray?
options: The left dome of the diaphragm
The right edge of the heart
questions.explanation: The middle lobe touches the right edge of the heart, so pneumonia there blurs that outline. This is the silhouette sign.

content.origin: From the Greek for a rounded flap, and the Latin for lower.
content.location: It is the lower back part of the right lung, below and behind the oblique fissure. Its base rests on the right dome of the diaphragm.
content.description: A big lobe that makes up most of the back of the right lung. It has five segments, one at the top and four at the base.
content.function: It handles gas exchange, taking in oxygen and letting out carbon dioxide. Its breath sounds are loudest on the lower back.
content.mnemonic: Lower lobes live at the back, so listen to them from behind.
content.clinical: When an upright person breathes in food or fluid, it most often lands here. It simply follows the straight right main bronchus downhill.
content.hint: Find the large back-and-bottom lobe on the right, sitting on the diaphragm behind the slanting fissure.

questions.text: In a person sitting upright, breathed-in fluid most often enters which lobe?
questions.explanation: Breathed-in material slides down the wide, upright right main bronchus and lands in the right lower lobe.

questions.text: The base of the right lower lobe rests on which structure?
questions.explanation: The lower lobes sit on the domes of the diaphragm, your big breathing muscle.

content.origin: From the Greek for a rounded flap. Its small flap, the lingula, is Latin for little tongue.
content.location: It is the top and front of the left lung. Its tip rises above the collarbone, and its front edge has a scoop for the heart, the cardiac notch.
content.description: The left lung has only two lobes, because the heart takes up room on that side. This upper lobe has a tongue-shaped flap below the notch, the lingula.
content.function: It swaps oxygen and carbon dioxide like every lobe. Its lingula lies over the front of the heart.
content.mnemonic: Left lung: two lobes, one fissure, a notch for the heart and a little tongue.
content.clinical: Pneumonia in the lingula can blur the left edge of the heart on a chest X-ray. This is called the silhouette sign.
content.hint: Find the top and front lobe on the left, with a scoop for the heart and a tongue-shaped flap below it.

content.origin: From the Greek for a rounded flap, and the Latin for lower.
content.location: It is the lower back part of the left lung, below and behind the oblique fissure. Its base rests on the left dome of the diaphragm.
content.description: It makes up most of the back and base of the left lung. Like the right lower lobe, it has one segment at the top and several at the base.
content.function: It handles gas exchange, like every lobe. Its breath sounds are loudest on the lower back.
content.mnemonic: Lower lobes live at the back, so listen from behind, low down on the back.
content.clinical: Fluid around the lungs, a pleural effusion, pools at the bases first. Tapping the lower back then sounds dull instead of hollow.
content.hint: Find the back-and-bottom lobe on the left, sitting on the diaphragm behind that lung's only fissure.

content.origin: From the Greek word for a partition or wall. It divides your chest from your belly.
content.location: It is a dome-shaped sheet between the chest and the abdomen, under the lungs and heart. The right dome sits a little higher because the liver lies beneath it.
content.description: Muscle around the edge meets in a tough central tendon, like a parachute canopy. Openings at the eighth, tenth and twelfth chest vertebrae let the vena cava, food pipe and aorta through.
content.function: It is your main breathing-in muscle. When it tightens, it flattens and moves down, making the chest bigger so air rushes into your lungs.
content.mnemonic: C three, four, five keeps the diaphragm alive, naming the neck nerves of the phrenic nerve. For the openings: I ate ten eggs at twelve, for vena cava, oesophagus and aorta.
content.clinical: A hiatus hernia is when part of the stomach pushes up through the opening for the food pipe. Hiccups are sudden, unplanned twitches of this muscle.
content.hint: Find the dome-shaped muscle under the lungs, separating the chest from the belly.

questions.text: What does the diaphragm do when it contracts?
options: Flattens and moves down, drawing air in
questions.explanation: When it tightens, the diaphragm flattens and moves down. The chest gets bigger and air flows in.
The phrenic nerve powers the diaphragm. It comes from the third to fifth neck nerves: C three, four, five keeps the diaphragm alive.
